analysis.one_liner: Restores net neutrality rules against blocking lawful content, while limiting FCC authority and preempting state internet laws.
analysis.headline: A net neutrality bill sponsored by a single Republican and cosponsored by nobody died in the Senate Commerce Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: In March 2018, Sen. John Kennedy (R-LA) introduced the Open Internet Preservation Act. It would have written open-internet protections into law: broadband providers could not block lawful content, applications, services, or devices (S2, S3). It came in response to the FCC's 2017 decision to repeal its 2015 net neutrality rules, so the bill would have preserved the core consumer protections while keeping broadband lightly regulated rather than reclassifying it as a common-carrier service. But it also would have tied regulators' hands: the FCC would enforce the rules case-by-case through complaint procedures with deadlines and could not act "by rulemaking or otherwise" beyond that, and the bill would preempt state laws on internet openness (S3). The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day it was introduced (S5). It never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote. No senator from either party cosponsored it (S4). It expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 (S5).
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses the internet. If it had passed, broadband customers would have enforceable federal protection against their provider blocking lawful websites, apps, services, or devices, enforced through FCC complaint procedures with firm deadlines (S2, S3). Internet content and streaming companies that depend on reaching users without paying carriers for access would also benefit.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit broadband internet access providers from blocking lawful content, applications, services, or non-harmful devices, restoring the core open-internet protections the FCC had adopted in 2015 and moved to repeal in 2017.

It would create FCC complaint procedures with a deadline of no more than 60 days after enactment, giving internet users a defined way to challenge a provider's conduct rather than relying on an agency choosing to act.
By writing the rules into statute instead of relying on FCC regulation, the protections would have been much harder for a future commission to reverse on its own.

analysis.who_pays: Broadband providers, who would be barred from blocking lawful content and from the related practices the bill restricts, and who would lose the ability to strike different deals with different internet companies. State governments would also lose authority to set their own rules, since the bill preempts state law on internet openness except for emergency communications and law enforcement needs (S3).

drawbacks.text: The bill would preempt state and local internet-openness rules (except for emergency communications and law enforcement), which would strip states of the ability to set stricter net neutrality protections of their own — a serious loss for consumers in states that wanted stronger rules.

The FCC would enforce the rules mainly through case-by-case complaints and could not act 'by rulemaking or otherwise' beyond that, so a user would have to file a complaint and win before a provider's conduct stopped, instead of a bright-line rule applying in advance.

The bill allows providers to offer 'specialized services' over the same network that share capacity with regular broadband, a carve-out critics warn can open the door to a two-tier internet favoring companies that pay for better treatment.

The strongest objection from the broadband industry's side, and one an honest supporter would have to acknowledge, is that restricting how providers manage and monetize their networks could reduce incentives to invest in network capacity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On the consumer side, this would have been a real but deliberately modest safeguard: it restored the anti-blocking protections users lost when the FCC reversed its 2015 rules, but it did so in a form broadband providers could live with — complaint-based enforcement rather than forward-looking rulemaking, no reclassification of broadband, and a federal ceiling that preempts stricter state laws. The cost is that the protections would be slower and weaker to invoke, and consumers in states wanting tougher rules would get the national floor instead. The bill was never tested: it died in committee with zero cosponsors, so no actual weighing of these tradeoffs ever occurred.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in March 2018, and that is where the record ends — no hearing, no markup, no vote, and it expired with the 115th Congress in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. John Kennedy introduced the bill on March 7, 2018, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
The committee never reported the bill; the full action history shows no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote after the referral.
No senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor during the bill's life.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill died with it, leaving the FCC's 2017 reversal of the 2015 open-internet rules in place.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large broadband providers. Because the bill died without any action, the anti-blocking protections it would have created never became law, the FCC's 2017 repeal of its 2015 rules stood, and providers kept their freedom to manage traffic and make paid deals — while states remained free to act on their own only because no federal preemption was enacted either.

for.name: Sen. John Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Open Internet Preservation Act, the only senator to attach his name to it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation (chaired by Sen. John Thune, R-SD)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no report.

against.name: Broadband industry (major cable and telecom providers and their trade associations)
against.what_they_did: Fought the return of net neutrality mandates after the FCC's 2017 repeal, which this bill would have partially codified.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no party breakdown exists in the record. The bill's sole sponsor was a Republican, no senator from either party cosponsored it (S4), and it died without action in a Republican-chaired committee (S5) — though Republican leadership's general opposition to restoring the FCC's 2015 rules and Democratic support for a stronger version shaped the environment in which nobody picked it up.

industries.industry: Broadband internet providers (cable and telecom carriers such as Comcast, AT&T, Verizon, and Charter)
industries.note: The bill would bar providers from blocking lawful content, applications, services, or devices, conduct they were free to resume after the FCC's 2017 repeal. It would also have capped their exposure, however: complaint-based enforcement instead of rulemaking, no reclassification as a common carrier, and federal preemption of stricter state rules — so this was a lighter-touch version of the rules they opposed.

industries.industry: Internet content, streaming, and app companies
industries.note: These companies depend on reaching users without carriers blocking or degrading their traffic; a statutory anti-blocking rule with defined complaint procedures would protect that access.
The bill preempts state and local internet-openness rules except for emergency communications and law enforcement, taking away states' ability to enact their own net neutrality protections.
